question: Your own voice on a recording sounds thinner and higher than you expect. What extra route does your voice normally take to your ears that the microphone never hears?
source_excerpt: your own voice reaches your inner ear two ways: through the air, like everyone else's, and through your skull.

extra.why_interesting: Almost everyone has cringed at their recorded voice and assumed the microphone distorts it. The twist is that the recording is what everyone else hears, and the 'real' voice in your head is the distorted one.
extra.verification_notes: Bone conduction through the skull adds low-frequency energy that microphones miss, as explained in the Popular Science article.

explanation: When you speak, vibrations travel through the bones of your skull and add a deeper, richer tone. The recording is what everyone else has been hearing all along.

question: True or false: when the full Moon looks huge rising over the horizon, a photo of it will show it clearly bigger than when it is high in the sky later that night.
source_excerpt: photographs of the Moon at different elevations also show that its size remains the same

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has seen a giant rising Moon and assumes it really is bigger, closer, or magnified by the atmosphere. A camera shows the size doesn't change. The enlargement happens in your brain.
extra.verification_notes: Photos at the same zoom show the Moon at the same angular size (~0.5°) near the horizon and high up; the horizon Moon looking bigger is a perceptual illusion (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_illusion).

explanation: False. In photos it is the same size, and actually a touch smaller, because on the horizon you are about 6,400 km farther from it. The giant Moon is an illusion created by your brain.
